## Overview

Backpressure in a streaming pipeline is the mechanism by which a slow downstream consumer signals an upstream producer to reduce its emission rate, rather than letting an unbounded buffer grow until the process runs out of memory.

Without backpressure, a fast producer can overwhelm a slow consumer, causing buffers to grow without bound and eventually exhausting memory resources. Backpressure ensures that data flow is controlled and aligned with the actual consumption capacity of the downstream system.

## Common Implementations

### Bounded Queues

A bounded queue implementation restricts the size of the buffer between producer and consumer. Once the queue reaches its maximum capacity, the producer is blocked (or paused) from adding new items until the consumer processes items and frees up space. This naturally throttles the producer's emission rate to match the consumer's consumption rate.

### Credit-Based Flow Control

In credit-based systems, the consumer explicitly grants the producer permission to send N more items by issuing "credits." The producer can only emit items if it has available credits; as the consumer processes items, it returns credits to the producer, allowing further emission. This model provides fine-grained control over flow rate and is commonly used in distributed systems and reactive frameworks.

### Reactive-Pull Models

Rather than the producer pushing items to the consumer, a reactive-pull model inverts control: the consumer requests items on its own schedule. The producer only emits when asked, ensuring that data flows at the pace the consumer can actually handle. This is the fundamental approach used in reactive programming libraries and pull-based streaming systems.

## Significance

Backpressure is essential for building robust, memory-efficient streaming systems that can gracefully handle mismatches in processing speed between pipeline stages. It prevents resource exhaustion and enables stable, predictable system behavior under load.
